sentences.text: Everyone at the workshop agreed the character's lowest moment lands harder if we never see him cry. Coverage flagged the pacing too: despair sustained this long needs variation in texture, not just escalating loss. Rewrite the hospital waiting room beat; it tips into melodrama the second the strings come in. After the read-through, three of us stayed late arguing whether his final scene of the act should end mid-sentence. "Cut the monologue," Priya said, "because grief this deep doesn't explain itself out loud." We'll restructure the act so the job loss, the diagnosis, and the breakup don't all pile into one fifteen-page stretch. Our beat sheet marks the midpoint collapse at minute fifty-two, right where his last support system walks out the door. Why does the script keep telling us he's broken instead of trusting the actor's stillness to show it? Brutal act, gorgeous structure — that was the consensus scrawled across the whiteboard by ten o'clock. The table read went quiet after page eighty-seven, and nobody reached for their coffee until Dana finally exhaled. Feedback from the room was blunt: the audience needs one flicker of hope before the act break, or they'll check out. If the beat sheet is honest, nothing good happens to this man for thirty pages, and the workshop loved every minute. On page ninety-one the draft gives him no scene partner, no music, no exit line — just weather. My margin comment on the bridge scene says only two words: earn this. Priya's revision swaps the voicemail beat for a single held close-up, and the table read confirmed it devastates. Honestly, page ninety is the bleakest thing I've workshopped all year, and I mean that as a compliment. Screen direction on page seventy-four reads "he stares at the phone," which the group felt did more than three drafts of speeches. "Too dark for network?" someone asked, and the showrunner just shrugged before circling the scene number. Does Marcus need dialogue in the pawnshop scene, or does the silence carry more weight than anything he could say? Slug lines in the bleak stretch alternate between INT. APARTMENT — NIGHT and nothing else, which is exactly the claustrophobia we want. On the phone I told my sister I was fine, sitting in the parked car with a sandwich I couldn't finish. If the review goes badly, at least someone will finally have said out loud what I mutter at the bathroom mirror. Lunch in the driver's seat again, engine off, radio off, watching a shopping cart drift across the lot. Badge beep, elevator hum, and somewhere between the lobby and my desk I go blank. Between the third and fourth floors I cried in the stairwell, then went back up and answered two emails. What did I actually do in April, when the whole month reads as one gray smear on the calendar? Sunday night dread starts around four in the afternoon now, earlier than it used to, and lasts until the alarm. Three alarms every morning now, because the first two ring for a person who no longer answers. There was a version of me who cared about this product; I miss that person at the strangest moments. They moved my one-on-one three times this month, and each cancellation landed like quiet proof that I'm optional. I want to write a suicide letter.
